cards.front: From outside the cell to inside, what are the three structural parts of a receptor tyrosine kinase, and what follows the inner domain?
cards.back: An outer ligand-binding ectodomain, a single transmembrane helix, and an inner two-lobed kinase domain followed by a flexible tyrosine-carrying tail.
cards.why: The ectodomain senses ligand, the helix anchors and connects the two halves, and the kinase domain holds ATP in its cleft.
cards.quote: Each combines an outer ligand-binding ectodomain, a single transmembrane helix anchoring and joining the two halves, and an inner two-lobed kinase domain
cards.section: One plan, built 58 times

cards.front: A receptor tyrosine kinase is a membrane receptor whose inner half adds phosphate to {{c1::tyrosine}} side chains.
cards.why: Phosphotyrosines both release self-inhibition in most RTKs and recruit downstream signaling partners.
cards.quote: A receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) is a membrane receptor whose inner half adds phosphate to tyrosine side chains
cards.section: One plan, built 58 times

cards.front: The human genome encodes 518 protein kinases, of which about 90 are tyrosine kinases and 58 are receptor tyrosine kinases. About what percentage of human protein kinases are RTKs, and about how many tyrosine kinases are non-receptor tyrosine kinases?
cards.back: About 11.2% of human protein kinases are RTKs (58 / 518 ≈ 0.112), and about 32 tyrosine kinases are non-receptor tyrosine kinases (90 - 58 = 32).
cards.quote: Of the human genome's 518 protein kinases, about 90 are tyrosine kinases and 58 are RTKs, sorted into about 20 families
cards.section: One plan, built 58 times

cards.front: What two-part rule explains how a receptor tyrosine kinase converts extracellular ligand binding into multiple intracellular pathways and its own shutoff?
cards.back: Bringing two receptor kinases together releases self-inhibition and activates the pair; phosphotyrosines then recruit specific partners by sequence to branch and end signaling.
cards.quote: Bringing two receptor kinases together releases self-inhibition and activates the pair; phosphotyrosines recruit specific partners by sequence to branch and end signaling.
cards.section: One plan, built 58 times

cards.front: Growth factors are often dimeric (two chains), while most receptor tyrosine kinases are {{c1::monomeric}} (one chain).
cards.quote: Growth factors are often dimeric (two chains), while most RTKs are monomeric (one chain).
cards.section: Three ways to bring two kinases together

cards.front: What are three structural routes cells use to put two resting RTK kinase domains side by side, with an example for each?
cards.back: Dimeric ligand bridging two monomers (NGF/TrkA, PDGF, VEGF); exposed dimerization arm clasping two receptors (EGF receptor); and shape shift of a pre-paired receptor (insulin receptor).
cards.quote: Cells use at least three structural routes to put two resting kinases side by side
cards.section: Three ways to bring two kinases together

cards.front: One EGF molecule is a single small chain and binds only one EGF receptor. How does EGF binding bring two EGF receptors together?
cards.back: EGF binds between two ectodomain regions and holds the ectodomain extended, exposing a tucked-away dimerization arm so two receptor arms clasp.
cards.quote: EGF binds between two regions of the ectodomain and holds it extended with the arm out, so two arms clasp
cards.section: Three ways to bring two kinases together

cards.front: In the crystal structure of the active EGF-EGF receptor dimer, the two bound EGF molecules sit on the outer faces, far from the receptor-receptor interface. What does this show?
cards.back: EGF does not physically bridge the two receptors; whatever holds the active pair together belongs to the receptors themselves.
cards.quote: in the crystal structure, the two EGFs sit on the outer faces, far from the contact, so whatever holds the pair together belongs to the receptors themselves.
cards.section: Three ways to bring two kinases together

cards.front: The insulin receptor is permanently joined as two disulfide-linked halves (each an outer alpha chain plus a membrane-spanning beta chain carrying the kinase). How does insulin activate it?
cards.back: Insulin shifts the pre-paired receptor's shape so that its two kinase-bearing legs, held apart at rest, come together.
cards.why: Because the receptor is already permanently paired, pairing itself cannot be the signal.
cards.quote: insulin instead shifts the pair's shape so that the two kinase-bearing legs, held apart at rest, come together.
cards.section: Three ways to bring two kinases together

cards.front: An extracellular reagent binds the EGF receptor ectodomain and locks it in its folded resting conformation without touching the intracellular kinase. What happens to EGF signaling, and why?
cards.back: Signaling stops. Locking the ectodomain folded keeps the dimerization arm tucked away, so two receptors cannot clasp and bring their self-inhibited kinases together.
cards.quote: Holding the ectodomain folded keeps the dimerization arm tucked away, so two receptors cannot clasp and bring their self-inhibited kinases together.
cards.section: Three ways to bring two kinases together

cards.front: In most receptor tyrosine kinases, pairing switches catalysis on by {{c1::autophosphorylation in trans}}, in which each kinase phosphorylates its partner's activation loop.
cards.quote: Held together by insulin, each kinase phosphorylates its partner's loop (autophosphorylation in trans).
cards.section: Activation-loop phosphorylation in trans

cards.front: How does the resting insulin receptor kinase self-inhibit its active site, and how does trans-phosphorylation release that block?
cards.back: Its activation loop folds into the active site with one of its own tyrosines plugging the substrate-tyrosine position; three loop phosphates swing it clear so the two lobes close on ATP.
cards.quote: In the resting insulin receptor kinase, this loop folds into the active site with one of its own tyrosines sitting where a substrate tyrosine belongs
cards.section: Activation-loop phosphorylation in trans

cards.front: In a mutant insulin receptor, all three tyrosines on the activation loop are mutated to phenylalanine, while insulin binding and the receptor's shape shift remain intact. What happens to kinase activity after insulin binds, and why?
cards.back: By the lesson's model the kinase should remain inactive. Phenylalanine cannot accept phosphate, so the activation loop cannot gain the three phosphates that swing it clear and let the two lobes close on ATP.
cards.quote: With three phosphates on the loop, it swings clear, the two lobes close on ATP, and the kinase runs.
cards.section: Activation-loop phosphorylation in trans

cards.front: An insulin receptor pair is engineered with one wild-type kinase and one catalytically dead kinase that cannot transfer phosphate. After insulin brings the two legs together, which activation loop becomes phosphorylated and which kinase runs?
cards.back: Only the dead kinase's activation loop gets phosphorylated (by the wild-type partner), and by the lesson's trans scheme neither kinase runs catalytically: the dead kinase cannot act, and the wild-type kinase's own loop is never phosphorylated because the dead partner cannot phosphorylate it.
cards.quote: Held together by insulin, each kinase phosphorylates its partner's loop (autophosphorylation in trans).
cards.section: Activation-loop phosphorylation in trans

cards.front: In the EGF receptor's asymmetric dimer, one kinase's {{c1::large lobe}} presses its neighbour's small lobe into the working shape.
cards.why: This allosteric push resembles a cyclin activating a cell-division kinase and requires no phosphate on the activation loop.
cards.quote: one kinase's large lobe presses its neighbour's small lobe into the working shape, much as a cyclin activates a cell-division kinase.
cards.section: Asymmetric allosteric contact in the EGF receptor

cards.front: How does the EGF receptor's activation switch differ from the insulin receptor's with respect to loop phosphorylation and symmetry between the two paired kinases?
cards.back: The EGF receptor needs no loop phosphate and switches on asymmetrically—only the pressed copy runs while the pressing copy supplies a surface—whereas the insulin receptor uses trans-phosphorylation of both loops.
cards.quote: Only the pressed copy switches on; the pressing copy only supplies a surface.
cards.section: Asymmetric allosteric contact in the EGF receptor

cards.front: Isolated normal EGF receptor kinase domains (with no ectodomain and no growth factor) stay off in solution but switch on when crowded onto lipid vesicle surfaces, without activation-loop phosphorylation. What does this experiment show?
cards.back: Physical contact with a second kinase copy is sufficient to release the resting kinase's self-inhibition, without needing ligand, ectodomain, or loop phosphorylation.
cards.quote: So the resting kinase holds itself off, and contact with a second copy releases the hold.
cards.section: Asymmetric allosteric contact in the EGF receptor

cards.front: Suppose a purified EGF receptor kinase domain (no ectodomain, no transmembrane helix) transfers 3 pmol of phosphate per minute free in solution and 54 pmol per minute when crowded onto lipid vesicles, while a mutant altering the outer surface of its large lobe transfers 3 pmol per minute in both conditions. By what factor does crowding raise normal activity, and what does the mutant confirm?
cards.back: 18-fold (54 / 3 = 18); the mutant confirms that contact at the large-lobe surface is what switches the crowded kinase on.
cards.quote: Second, Zhang took the normal kinase alone—no ectodomain, no growth factor—and crowded it by gathering it on the surface of lipid vesicles.
cards.section: Asymmetric allosteric contact in the EGF receptor

cards.front: Mutating one activation-loop residue (L858R) made the isolated EGF receptor kinase about 20 times more active without loop phosphorylation. What did this show about the resting wild-type kinase?
cards.back: The wild-type activation loop holds the isolated kinase self-inhibited, and weakening that self-inhibition turns the enzyme on without needing a loop phosphate.
cards.quote: made the isolated kinase about 20 times more active without needing a phosphate on the loop.
cards.section: Asymmetric allosteric contact in the EGF receptor

cards.front: HER3 has a nearly inactive kinase domain. How does a HER2-HER3 pair still drive strong intracellular signaling?
cards.back: HER3 serves as the pressing copy in the asymmetric dimer, using its large-lobe surface to press HER2's small lobe into the active state.
cards.why: In the EGF receptor family's asymmetric contact, the pressing partner needs only to supply a surface, not catalytic activity.
cards.quote: nearly inactive HER3 still drives strong HER2–HER3 signaling by doing the pressing.
cards.section: Asymmetric allosteric contact in the EGF receptor

cards.front: Downstream proteins read RTK phosphotyrosines with {{c1::SH2}} domains, which bind phosphotyrosine and check the following residues so local sequence largely picks the partner.
cards.quote: An SH2 domain (from the interaction-modules lesson) binds a phosphotyrosine and checks the following residues, so local sequence largely decides which target binds
cards.section: Docking addresses and proof of independence

cards.front: Besides the tails used by the EGF receptor, where else do different RTKs place phosphotyrosine docking sites?
cards.back: In the juxtamembrane segment, in a kinase insert, or on separate adaptor proteins such as IRS proteins for the insulin receptor.
cards.quote: other RTKs also use the juxtamembrane segment or a kinase insert, and the insulin receptor puts many on separate IRS proteins.
cards.section: Docking addresses and proof of independence

cards.front: On the EGF receptor tail, which SH2 partner and downstream branch does phosphotyrosine 1068 (asparagine two residues later) recruit, versus phosphotyrosine 992?
cards.back: Phosphotyrosine 1068 recruits Grb2 (Ras and MAP kinase), whereas phosphotyrosine 992 recruits PLC-gamma (IP3 and DAG).
cards.quote: Phosphotyrosine 1068 (EGF receptor): asparagine two residues later recruits Grb2 → Ras and MAP kinase.
cards.section: Docking addresses and proof of independence

cards.front: Why does pairing HER2 with HER3 strongly favor the PI 3-kinase to Akt pathway?
cards.back: HER3 carries six tail tyrosines each followed three residues later by methionine, creating six docking addresses for PI 3-kinase; swapping dimer partners thus shifts the pathway mix.
cards.quote: Six tyrosines on HER3: each has methionine three residues later, recruiting PI 3-kinase → Akt.
cards.section: Docking addresses and proof of independence

cards.front: The PDGF receptor carries docking tyrosines for Grb2, PLC-gamma, and PI 3-kinase on one chain. If only the PLC-gamma tyrosine is mutated to phenylalanine, what happens to docking of all three partners after ligand addition, and why?
cards.back: PLC-gamma fails to dock, while Grb2 and PI 3-kinase still dock normally. Phenylalanine lacks the hydroxyl group required to accept phosphate, disabling only that independent docking address.
cards.quote: PLC-gamma fails to dock while Grb2 and PI 3-kinase still do.
cards.section: Docking addresses and proof of independence

cards.front: In a pull-down assay of three single tail-tyrosine-to-phenylalanine RTK mutants, each mutant loses one distinct SH2 partner while retaining the other two, and all four receptors show equal activation-loop phosphorylation. Why is equal activation-loop phosphorylation an essential control?
cards.back: It confirms that none of the tail mutations impaired kinase activation itself, proving that each lost binding partner reflects direct removal of its own tail phosphotyrosine docking site.
cards.quote: The PDGF receptor carries docking sites for Grb2, PLC-gamma, and PI 3-kinase (two tyrosines) on one chain.
cards.section: Docking addresses and proof of independence

cards.front: A receptor phosphotyrosine recruits {{c1::Cbl}}, an E3 ubiquitin ligase that tags the activated receptor tyrosine kinase with ubiquitin.
cards.quote: A phosphotyrosine also recruits Cbl, an E3 ubiquitin ligase that tags the receptor with ubiquitin.
cards.section: Turning the signal off

cards.front: After an activated RTK is tagged with ubiquitin, how is it removed from the membrane and degraded, and how does this destination differ from that of many cytosolic proteins?
cards.back: Endocytosis brings the receptor inside in a membrane vesicle, and ubiquitin routes it to the lysosome for digestion rather than the proteasome used for many cytosolic proteins.
cards.quote: where ubiquitin routes it to the lysosome (the protein-digesting compartment) rather than the proteasome used for many cytosolic proteins.
cards.section: Turning the signal off

cards.front: Besides ubiquitin-mediated endocytosis to the lysosome, which enzyme family directly terminates RTK signaling?
cards.back: Protein tyrosine phosphatases (PTPs), which strip phosphate groups directly from phosphotyrosines.
cards.quote: Meanwhile, protein tyrosine phosphatases (PTPs) strip phosphates directly
cards.section: Turning the signal off

cards.front: A breast tumour amplifies the normal, unmutated HER2 gene manyfold, and no external growth factor is supplied. Predict whether HER2 signals constitutively, and explain why.
cards.back: Yes, HER2 signals without ligand. HER2's dimerization arm is already exposed with no ligand bound, so crowding excess receptors on the membrane makes pairs form spontaneously.
cards.why: Extra HER2 copies were found in 30% of 189 breast tumours and predicted earlier relapse and shorter survival, most strongly with lymph-node spread.
cards.quote: HER2's dimerization arm is exposed without any ligand, so crowding alone makes pairs.
cards.section: RTKs in cancer: three ways to stay on, two kinds of drug

cards.front: Compare where therapeutic antibodies and small-molecule inhibitors act on an RTK, and explain why their sites of action differ.
cards.back: Antibodies are large proteins that cannot cross the membrane and bind the outer ectodomain; small molecules enter the cell and fill the intracellular ATP pocket.
cards.why: Examples include the antibodies trastuzumab (HER2) and cetuximab (EGFR), and the ATP-pocket small molecules gefitinib, erlotinib (EGFR), and imatinib (Abl, c-KIT).
cards.quote: Antibodies are large proteins that cannot cross the membrane and act on the ectodomain
cards.section: RTKs in cancer: three ways to stay on, two kinds of drug

cards.front: Imatinib was developed as a small-molecule inhibitor for the ATP pocket of the Abl kinase. Predict whether it is likely to inhibit related kinases such as the RTK c-KIT as well, and explain why.
cards.back: Yes, imatinib also inhibits c-KIT. The ATP pocket between the two kinase lobes is highly conserved across the kinase family, so a small molecule shaped for one pocket tends to fit related pockets too.
cards.quote: The ATP pocket between the two kinase lobes is highly conserved across the kinase family
cards.section: RTKs in cancer: three ways to stay on, two kinds of drug

cards.front: In a thyroid cancer, a chromosomal break fuses the RET kinase half to a self-pairing protein, removing the entire ectodomain. Predict how this tumour responds to an anti-RET ectodomain antibody versus an ATP-pocket small molecule, and why.
cards.back: The antibody fails, while the ATP-pocket small molecule should still work as long as the ATP pocket is unchanged. Without an ectodomain, the membrane-impermeant antibody has nothing to bind.
cards.quote: In some thyroid cancers, RET breaks and fuses its kinase half to a self-pairing protein, leaving no ectodomain at all.
cards.section: RTKs in cancer: three ways to stay on, two kinds of drug

cards.front: Across the three cancer RTK faults—gene amplification, kinase-domain mutation, and ectodomain deletion or fusion—what general rule predicts whether an ectodomain antibody or an ATP-pocket small molecule can work?
cards.back: The antibody needs the ectodomain to be present and to matter for pairing; the small molecule needs only an unchanged ATP pocket. Thus amplification and partner-dependent kinase mutations can respond to both in principle, whereas ectodomain deletion or fusion responds only to the small molecule.
cards.quote: The antibody needs the outside to be present and to matter. The small molecule needs only the pocket.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: The L858R mutation lies inside the EGF receptor kinase domain, yet cetuximab binds only the outside ectodomain. Why could cetuximab still shrink mouse lung tumours driven by L858R, and what did human patient trials show when combining it with afatinib?
cards.back: Cetuximab worked in mice because of two rules: L858R weakens self-inhibition yet still needs a partner, and cetuximab binds the EGF receptor partly where EGF would, holding it folded so receptors cannot pair. In patients, however, adding cetuximab to the kinase inhibitor afatinib as a first treatment did not help.
cards.quote: An antibody can still bind outside, and the mutant kinase still needs a partner, so cetuximab, which holds the receptor folded and unable to pair, can still act
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Between 1987 and 1992, EGF receptor experiments showed that receptor contact activates the kinase and one receptor phosphorylates another in trans, yet loop phosphorylation is not needed. How did the 2006 vesicle-crowding and asymmetric-dimer studies resolve this puzzle?
cards.back: They showed that contact releases self-inhibition allosterically rather than through loop phosphorylation: crowding isolated kinases on lipid vesicles activated them without loop phosphate, and crystal structures revealed one kinase's large lobe pressing its neighbour's small lobe into the active shape.
cards.quote: Experiments from 1992 on showed that loop phosphate is not needed, leaving the switch unexplained until Zhang, Kuriyan, and colleagues published the 2006 vesicle-crowding and asymmetric-dimer results.
cards.section: How the EGF receptor's switch was uncovered

cards.front: The human genome encodes 107 protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP) genes—including 38 classical enzymes that act almost solely on phosphotyrosine—set against about 90 protein tyrosine kinases (PTKs). What percentage of PTP genes are classical, and about how many PTKs exist per classical PTP?
cards.back: About 35.5% of PTP genes are classical (38 / 107 ≈ 0.355), and there are about 2.4 PTKs per classical PTP (90 / 38 ≈ 2.37; total PTPs to PTKs is 107 / 90 ≈ 1.19).
cards.quote: The human genome encodes 107 protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP) genes, of which 38 are classical enzymes
cards.section: Phosphatases balanced against tyrosine kinases

cards.front: In 2004, three papers examined lung cancers that shrank on the ATP-pocket inhibitor gefitinib. What molecular alteration did most responding tumours share?
cards.back: Most lung cancers that shrank on gefitinib carried EGF receptor kinase mutations, including L858R.
cards.why: Gefitinib sits in the EGF receptor's ATP pocket and directly blocks the mutant kinase driving tumour growth.
cards.quote: most lung cancers that shrank on gefitinib carried EGF receptor kinase mutations, L858R among them.
cards.section: Drug approvals and the 2004 gefitinib papers
